shape, size and ndim.syntax: a.shape → tuple   |   a.size → int   |   a.ndim → int
steps: Build the 2×3 array and print all three attributes in one call.
Read shape as (rows, columns) and check size is their product.
Count the entries of shape to confirm ndim.
shape, size and ndim.visual:
a.shape = (2, 3)   rows × columns
a.size  = 6        cells
a.ndim  = 2        number of axes
shape, size and ndim.realWorld: A model expects a feature matrix and fails on shape; printing shape, size and ndim first tells you whether the data is transposed or flattened.
mistakes: Reading shape as (columns, rows) and transposing the wrong way.
Using len(a) when the total cell count is what is needed.
revision: shape is the structure, size is the cell count, ndim is the axis count.

steps: Build an integer array and print dtype.
Print itemsize and note it is bytes per element, not per array.
Multiply itemsize by size to reach nbytes.
dtype and itemsize.visual:
dtype int64 → itemsize 8 bytes
3 elements  → nbytes 24
dtype and itemsize.realWorld: A million-row column of small integers costs 8 MB as int64 and 1 MB as int8 — the dtype decision is the memory decision.
mistakes: Assuming itemsize changes with array length.
Casting to a smaller dtype without checking the value range.
revision: dtype names the element type; itemsize is its width in bytes.

steps: Sum a 2×2 array with axis=0 and read the result shape.
Sum with axis=1 and compare which values disappeared.
Say out loud which axis vanished in each case.
Axis means the direction that is collaps.realWorld: Monthly sales per product: axis=0 totals each product across months, axis=1 totals each month across products.
mistakes: Thinking axis names the direction that stays.
Expecting the same shape back from a reduction.
revision: The named axis is the one removed.

steps: Build a 3×4 array and print len(a).
Compare it with a.size.
Use shape[0] and shape[1] when both counts matter.
len counts the first axis only.realWorld: Counting rows of a table is len(a); counting measured values is a.size — mixing them inflates sample counts.
mistakes: Assuming len gives the cell count.
Using len on a 0-d array and expecting 1.
revision: len is the first axis only.

steps: Build a 3×4 array and print both shapes.
Transpose and print the shape again.
Note that values were not reordered, only the axes were swapped.
Transpose swaps the shape.realWorld: A CSV read as (features, samples) usually needs .T before a model that expects (samples, features).
mistakes: Believing .T copies the data — it is a view with swapped strides.
Transposing twice and forgetting the data is back to the original.
revision: It is a view until something forces a copy.

steps: Build an array from an int and a float.
Print the dtype and observe both values became floats.
Pass dtype explicitly when the promotion is unwanted.
Mixed literals promote to float.realWorld: One decimal in a price column silently turns the whole column into floats, which changes equality and memory behaviour.
mistakes: Expecting the integer to stay an integer in a mixed array.
Relying on exact equality after promotion.
revision: Mixed input promotes to the common type.

steps: Create an array from a single number.
Print ndim and shape to see () and 0.
Use .item() to get the plain Python scalar back.
A zero-dimensional array has no axes.realWorld: A reduction over every axis returns a 0-d array; printing it looks like a number but it is still an ndarray.
mistakes: Indexing a 0-d array as if it had axes.
Comparing it to a Python int in a type check.

steps: Create a float32 array of shape (2, 3).
Print nbytes and square it against size × itemsize.
Repeat with float64 to see the memory double.
Bytes are shape times itemsize.realWorld: Choosing float32 for a large feature matrix halves memory and often changes nothing measurable in accuracy.
mistakes: Confusing nbytes with the Python object's overhead.
Forgetting that a copy doubles the count.
revision: dtype width is the multiplier you control.

steps: Create a three-axis array.
Print ndim and size, and confirm size is the product of shape.
Index with three positions to see each axis used.
ndim counts the axes.realWorld: An image batch is (batch, height, width) or (batch, height, width, channels) — ndim tells you which convention you are holding.
mistakes: Counting shape entries by eye and getting it wrong.
Assuming a 2-D model accepts a 3-D batch.
revision: Each axis needs its own index.

steps: Create ten zeros and print the shape.
Notice the trailing comma: one axis, ten cells.
Compare with np.zeros((10, 1)) which has two axes.
Ten zeros are one dimension.realWorld: A single feature column must be (n, 1) to broadcast as a column; (n,) silently broadcasts as a row.
mistakes: Treating (10,) and (10, 1) as the same shape.
Reshaping to (10,) and losing the column semantics.
revision: A 1-D shape is written with a trailing comma.

steps: Create a 2×2 array.
Read rows and columns from the tuple by position.
Use those values in a reshape or a loop bound.
Shape is a tuple you can index.realWorld: Building a result array with np.zeros(a.shape[0]) is how code stays correct when the row count changes.
mistakes: Indexing shape[1] on a 1-D array.
Assuming shape is a list and calling .append.

steps: Build a nested list with one inner list.
Print the shape and note the leading 1.
Compare with np.array([7, 8]) which is 1-D.
A matrix of one row still has two axes.realWorld: Batching a single sample for a model needs (1, features); passing (features,) is the classic shape error.
mistakes: Dropping the outer list and losing the batch axis.
Squeezing a batch of one to save memory and breaking the model call.
revision: Batch of one is still a batch.

Every attribute of an ndarray.syntax: shape · ndim · size · dtype · itemsize · nbytes · strides
steps: Reshape a range into a 3×4 array.
Print all attributes in one line.
Read strides as bytes to step per axis.
Every attribute of an ndarray.visual:
shape (3, 4) · size 12 · dtype int64
strides (32, 8) = 4 elements, then 1
Every attribute of an ndarray.realWorld: Disagreement between shape and strides is how a transposed view keeps the same buffer without copying.
mistakes: Reading strides in elements instead of bytes.
Assuming a reshape always changes strides.
revision: strides are byte steps per axis.
A view shares the buffer; strides differ.

steps: Create zeros to see a known starting state.
Create empty of the same shape and print its dtype and shape only.
Never print or rely on empty's values.
np.empty is not filled with zeros.realWorld: Preallocating an output buffer with empty is a legitimate speed trick — as long as every cell is written before it is read.
mistakes: Assuming empty contains zeros.
Reading an unwritten cell and treating garbage as data.
revision: Write every cell before reading it.
